claim: During the 2026-07-26 RustFS soak, enumeration of a ref-log stream returned `seq 0x1430e` while omitting predecessors `0x1430c` and `0x1430d`.
The two omitted ref-log objects were uploaded at 16:47:19, 2.2 ms apart, and the anomaly fired at 16:47:38, so both objects were durable for approximately 19 seconds before the anomaly.
An exact-key `HEAD` at the moment of the ref-log disagreement confirmed that each omitted key was present.
Across 65,263 ref-log uploads in the affected namespace, partitioned by epoch, zero uploads were out of order.
The 2026-07-26 RustFS incident was classified as a correct tail with omission of predecessors below the returned frontier, not as tail under-reporting.
Concurrent delete was excluded as an explanation for the RustFS ref-log omission.
Stale-epoch minting was excluded as an explanation for the RustFS ref-log omission.
Out-of-order appends were excluded as an explanation for the RustFS ref-log omission.
A late `Unresolved` PUT was excluded as an explanation for the RustFS ref-log omission.
On any contract-compliant S3, including AWS, omission of predecessors below a correct tail is legal when writes are concurrent with a paginated enumeration.
S3 read-after-write guarantees cover lists started after a `PUT` completes.
S3 provides no snapshot contract for keys that land during a paginated walk: a key landing behind the pagination marker can be invisible, while a later key ahead of the marker can be visible.
Arithmetic middle intake is mandatory everywhere; it is not a RustFS-specific workaround.
The observed RustFS instance was a contract violation under AWS-style semantics because the omitted keys had been durable for approximately 19 seconds before the enumeration began.
A contract-compliant store can produce the same omission shape only when the relevant writes are concurrent with the enumeration.
Tail under-reporting of a completed write is illegal on a contract-compliant store because of the read-after-write clause.
Tail under-reporting of a completed write is the only LIST property that a per-backend trust mode may rely on.
No LIST violation of any kind has been observed on AWS S3; the incident is evidence about RustFS and about what enumeration concurrency legally permits, not about AWS S3.
During the RustFS incident, exact-key `GET` and `HEAD` returned truthful presence information while LIST omitted keys.
Conditional writes are trusted by construction because a store cannot return `Created` for `putIfAbsent` on an existing key without destroying its own data.
The CAS GC trust chain is catalog cut for the universe, `_ckpt` for the acknowledged frontier, exact `GET`s for records, and conditional writes for fences.
LIST is used only as a hint for work bounds, witness sets, and genesis; a LIST lie in either direction can delay reclamation but cannot authorize destruction.
A stale-but-honest read represents a true cut from the past, so its errors move toward retention or delay rather than authorization.
Temporal arms close stale-read errors forward through a round-paced floor, exact-token delete, and delete-site in-degree re-read in `Gc/CasBlobInDegree.cpp`.
A fabricated cut caused by omission under a seal corresponds to no point in time; folding it and sealing above hidden records can authorize destruction, which is unrecoverable.
Delay-shaped errors are acceptable in CAS GC, while authorization-shaped errors are not.
Three hammer runs listed approximately 19 million keys with zero holes before a LIST violation fired live within four minutes of an ordinary RustFS soak.
The LIST failure is rare, depends on load and timing, and was not reproducible on demand.
A mount-time synthetic probe that puts a few keys, lists them, and compares the results will pass on virtually every store, including RustFS, so absence of probe evidence is not a backend passport.
A one-shot LIST-consistency probe cannot soundly certify a backend.
One valid passport is operator attestation per bucket that the bucket is AWS or GCS with documented strong LIST semantics, with the operator accepting the residual risk for that bucket.
LIST trust mode is a runtime property of a bucket, never a property of a backend type string.
Another valid passport is continuous verification with auto-revocation: retain trust while continuously sampling exact-key probes or `_ckpt`-versus-tail cross-checks.
The first observed LIST lie during continuous verification permanently demotes the bucket to probe-always and records an anomaly.
Sampling bounds detection time but does not bound exposure of unsampled namespaces during the detection window, so sampling is a risk-acceptance knob rather than proof.
Operator attestation and continuous verification can be combined, using attestation to enable trust and verification to revoke it.
The fail-close default is probe-always, and any doubt must select probe-always.
RustFS currently fails the LIST-trust passport based on measurement.
Arithmetic middle intake is required everywhere, including trusted backends.
Frontier probes remain necessary for held namespaces and for namespaces with no listed logs.
The condition `tail < cursor` continues to feed the store-quality detector.
Under a passport shaped as described in the probe limits, the only backend-gradeable claim is that `tail == cursor` proves the frontier.
The parallel-walk optimization is trust-neutral and does not require the LIST-trust passport.
